text:
I bought this second-hand mechanical keyboard for $38, so I wasn’t expecting perfection, and that is pretty much what I got. It arrived reasonably clean and worked right away, which was a relief. The typing feel is actually better than I expected for the price. I write a lot of long emails for work, and the keys are comfortable enough that my hands don’t feel tired after an hour or two.

There are a couple of issues, though. The space bar rattles noticeably, especially if I hit it near the edges, and it makes the whole board sound cheaper than it feels. Also, one key occasionally repeats, which is annoying when I’m typing quickly and have to go back to delete an extra letter. It doesn’t happen constantly, but it happens enough to mention.

The seller did answer my question about the switches, but it took a full week, by which point I had basically figured it out myself. I considered returning it, but for $38, shipping it back didn’t seem worth the trouble. Overall, I kept it because it is comfortable and usable, just not flawless.

I bought this second-hand mechanical keyboard for $38, so I wasn’t expecting a museum piece. Still, it’s better than I thought it’d be. The board has a nice weight to it, the keys feel satisfying without being too loud, and it’s genuinely comfortable for long emails. I’ve written several rambling work messages on it already, and my wrists haven’t complained, which is more than I can say for my old flat keyboard.

That said, it’s not perfect. The space bar rattles in a way that makes it sound cheaper than the rest of the board, especially if I’m typing fast. One key also occasionally repeats, which is annoying when I don’t catch it right away. Nothing catastrophic, but definitely noticeable.

The seller was fine, I guess, though they answered my question about the switches a full week late. By then, the keyboard had already arrived, so thanks for that, I suppose.

I considered shipping it back, but honestly, for $38, it wasn’t worth the hassle. I kept it. It’s flawed, slightly cranky, and somehow still useful.

I bought this keyboard used for $38, which felt fair as soon as I pulled it out of the box. It had a little dust between the keys and a few shiny spots on the caps, but nothing worse than I expected from a second-hand board.

The good part: it is genuinely comfortable. I write long emails for work, and my hands feel less cramped than they did on my flat office keyboard. The switches have a steady feel, not too heavy, and the case does not slide around on my desk.

There are problems. The space bar rattles every time I hit it, loud enough that I notice it during quiet mornings. One key, the “e,” occasionally repeats, so I get words like “neeed” if I type too fast. It does not happen constantly, but it happens enough that I proofread more carefully.

I also asked the seller what switches it had, and they answered a full week later, after the keyboard had already arrived. Not great.

Still, for $38, I kept it. Shipping it back felt like more trouble than the keyboard was worth.

I paid $38 for this second-hand mechanical keyboard, so my hope was modest: no missing keycaps, no sticky mystery grime, and switches that didn’t feel like gravel. On that scale, it did fine. It showed up clean enough to put on my desk without a deep-cleaning project, and the keys have a pleasant weight to them. I type a lot of long emails, and this board is genuinely comfortable for that. My fingers don’t feel beat up after a long stretch, which is more than I can say for some newer cheap keyboards.

The rough edges are not hidden. The space bar rattles every time I catch it off-center, a loose little clack that makes the whole board sound cheaper than it feels. One key also repeats now and then, so I’ll look up and find an extra letter sitting in the middle of a sentence. Not constant, but irritating.

Communication was another weak spot. I asked the seller what switches it had, and the answer came a week later, after I’d already pulled a keycap and checked for myself. I thought about returning it, then pictured packing it up and paying to ship it back. For $38, I kept it. It’s flawed, but usable.
